paragraphs: Yao Chang escaped Chang’an on the very night torches flared outside Murong Chui’s residence.

In later years he often remembered that drain. The palace gates of Chang’an had been rebuilt more than once, and the seals of the military offices had passed through many hands. Yet no one had cared to spend the money to fill an abandoned sewage channel in the western city. Thorny weeds grew on either bank. Whenever it rained, the reek of mud seeped through the cracks in the bricks and into the courtyard. The soldiers guarding the residence inspected every letter, visitor, and delivery of charcoal or rice. None imagined a passage under the wall.

As an old servant lifted the loose bricks, urgent hoofbeats sounded in the outer street. Yao Chang shed his neat blue robe and pulled on the short jacket of a dye-shop porter. He tried the bottom of the ditch with one foot. The foul mud rose over his ankle.
“My lord, shall we take your old armor?” The servant held out a worn leather cuirass. Stitches sewn by the Yao household years ago still showed at the shoulder.
Yao Chang looked at it for a moment, then pushed it back into the chest. “Carry that, and they’ll recognize me before we reach a checkpoint.”
“Out west they’ll know who’s come as soon as they see it.”
“If they cannot recognize the man, let them do without the armor.”

A lamp still burned in the room. Black and white stones lay scattered across a half-finished game of go. Before closing the door Yao Chang picked up a white stone and slipped it into his sleeve. The old servant asked why. Yao Chang said there was grease on two of his fingers and he had picked it up without thinking. After years in his service, the man knew that was no answer, but asked nothing more.

That night the different parties were each pursuing their own designs. Men bearing forged redeployment orders could not even name the officers supposedly issuing them. Several groups of clan retainers risked an assault on the arsenal, each with its own calculations. Yao Chang’s rescuers did no more than push a dyer’s cart into the ward while the streets were in confusion. When the ox cart stopped outside the drain, its driver was still quarreling with an inspecting guard about whether the barrels ought to be sealed with wax.

Yao Chang curled himself inside an empty indigo barrel, a wet cloth pressed against his shoulders and neck. A spear point entered the barrel’s side less than an inch from his ear. Cold water ran down his collar, and blue-black dye soaked into the gray at his temples. He held his breath. Outside, someone accused the driver of evading tax. The driver shouted back that the soldiers had punctured his barrel and would have to pay for it in the morning. At last came a slap on the cart’s boards, and the oxen moved again.

Leaving the city was harder than leaving the ward. The rescuers joined a convoy carrying corpses and used a genuine burial-ground exit permit to conceal Yao Chang beneath mats beside the dead. The pass was authentic, and three people on the cart really had died. The fourth had been a boy killed at a clan estate the night before; his body had been moved elsewhere at the last moment.

When the gate guard lifted the mat, Yao Chang lay with his eyes shut and cold ash over his face. The soldier touched the side of his neck and thought he felt warmth. The driver hastily explained that the dead man had taken poison and his body had not yet cooled. Repelled by the corpse and by the shouting queue of carts behind him, the guard let the mat fall back into place.

As the cartwheel crossed the threshold, Yao Chang heard the iron chain fastened again. He recalled the night long before when Fu Jian had collected the generals' tiger tallies, and the palace gates had shut just like that. He had laughed in the corridor then. Tonight he lay beside dead men. Nothing about it amused him.

More than twenty mounted men waited in a stand of bare trees. Yao Shuode had waited until his lips were cracked. The moment he saw Yao Chang, he bowed low and hailed him as lord. Yao Chang’s first question was, “How many places did they take in Chang’an?”
“The arsenal held. Murong Chui is still in his residence. Fu Hong’s men are already searching the clan estates.”
“And Fu Pi?”
“Still at Xiangyang.”
“Any report from Luoyang?”
“Only rumors that the Heavenly King has not awakened.”

By firelight Yao Chang burned the secret notes one by one. He lingered over one letter after reading it. Two branches of the imperial clan, it said, were quarreling over which should be first to take possession of the seals. At last he pressed a corner of the paper into the coals and watched the flame consume his own name.
“Westward.”
Yao Shuode asked whether they should immediately raise the old Yao banner. “Don’t let Chang’an raise our banner for us,” Yao Chang said.

They left the official road and traveled west along desolate slopes north of the Wei River, old salt-cart tracks, and wells used by shepherds. On the third day notices calling for his arrest appeared at the checkpoints. The painted Yao Chang had full cheeks and a groomed beard, the prosperous face of a man attending court in former years. A thin man in rough clothes paused before one poster and watched a child roll up its lower edge to make a toy tube. He lowered his hat brim and led his horse onward. Even the child paid him no attention.

Beyond the Jing River people began waiting by the road. At first one or two of his former followers; then groups of three or five riders, their saddles hung with dry grass and water skins. Some knelt at the sight of him. Others stared from a few paces away, trying to decide whether this gaunt old man could really be the renowned Qiang commander they remembered.

An old herdsman recognized him and would not release his reins. The man’s son had died the previous year in a dispute over the measurement of grazing land. County surveyors had come with their ropes and marked grassland where the family had grazed horses for generations as ownerless waste. They had no title deed, only an old wooden tag showing that their fathers and grandfathers had supplied horses to the army. The son had appealed, been knocked down by county soldiers, and died after twenty days of a festering wound.
“To whom did you deliver horses before?” Yao Chang asked.
“To the Yao household. Later, to the Qin army.”
“Did the county issue a receipt?”
“No. The military office recorded them.”

The old man drew a fistful of hardened earth from his clothes and thrust it into Yao Chang’s hand, trembling. “Here is my family’s deed. If anyone doubts it, let him ask the dead horses beneath the roots.”

Yao Chang took the earth. It was cold in his palm. He did not promise to kill officials or seize land in revenge. Instead, he asked the county deputy’s name and the date of the appeal and told Yao Shuode to write them down. The old man’s face brightened; he thought the general meant to avenge his son. But Yao Chang said, “Don’t kill him yet. If you do, the county ledgers may go up in flames.”
“My lord still means to examine Qin accounts?” the old man asked, bewildered.
“Yes.” Yao Chang returned the earth. “Otherwise you won’t even know whom to claim your due from.”

After they entered Anding, more and more petitioners arrived: military households whose compensation had been omitted from the new registers; mountain people whose pastures had been swallowed by local magnates; farmers made to pay the “river-defense grain levy” twice. There were tribal chiefs too, complaining that the court had deprived them of their fighting men and tax revenues. Yao Chang heard these groups separately. When one estate owner boasted that the government had stolen his ancestral fields, Yao asked where the tenant farmers of those days had gone. The man could not say. Yao Chang ordered him out. Though he had three hundred household troops at his back, the camp gate did not open for that petitioner.
In private Yao Shuode asked, “When you’re gathering an army, why offend men willing to give you money and horses?”
“Anyone can claim he was wronged. If I kill his enemy for him, next time he’ll ask me to kill someone else.”
“Does my lord not intend to contend for the realm?”
“That is exactly why I cannot promise everything to everyone.”

As he spoke, Yao Chang sat beside the earthen stove of a farmhouse, gnawing a hard flatbread. In Chang’an he had grown used to roast meat from the palace kitchens. This bread jarred his teeth. The old woman of the house recognized him as someone important, but asked nothing about affairs of state. She set a bowl of hot soup beside him. It had no salt and only a few floating wild greens. After two sips Yao Chang called her back. “How many sons do you have?”
“Three. One died, one went to serve as a soldier, and the one left has a lame leg.”
“Who will care for you when you’re old?”
The woman wiped the bowl with a cloth. “If the land stays ours, there’ll be no need for anyone to.”
He asked nothing more.

The grass in White Grass Valley was just turning green. It was a broad valley, low hills at either end holding back the wind, a spring stream winding through the middle. As the tribes arrived, they fought according to old custom for the camps nearest the water. The Yao family’s former followers pitched tents west of the stream, the Liang people east of it, and soldiers who had deserted the Qin army crowded the grassy slopes. From afar the multitude of banners looked like bright birds scattered over the plain; close up, the confusion was appalling. One tribe refused to lend horses, another chief refused to share cooking fires. A clerk who had fled government service tried to establish a grain ledger and was shouted down before he could begin.

Yao Chang’s first act on entering the camp was not to receive obeisance. He inspected a shipment of millet from Gaoping County. The sacks still bore the red seals of a Qin granary. The men unloading them argued that this was official grain and taking it counted as military merit. But in a corner of the yard a mother and daughter huddled together. The soldiers transporting the grain had also taken their cloth, and when the two went to ask for it they were knocked down.

Yao Chang ordered the cloth returned and the ringleader tied beneath a cart shaft. A tribal chief protested, “You cannot wound the spirits of men who’ve just come to you. These brothers risked their lives for your sake.”
“They haven’t fought a battle yet.” Yao Chang pointed to the mother and daughter. “If their first act is to rob one family of its winter cloth, how is White Grass Valley supposed to support an army?”
The chief was unconvinced. “When Qin soldiers came onto our pasture, they weren’t so scrupulous.”
“If I copy the worst of the Qin army, why should I ask you to follow me?”

Some men nodded; others nursed their anger. Yao Chang knew he had only checked the matter for now. Each tribe still held its own sacks of grain. Restoring a few lengths of cloth to an injured woman was easy. Taking an entire granary out of those chiefs' hands would be harder.

At dusk Yao Shuode brought the tribal rolls. One chief claimed five thousand men, but little more than two thousand actually drew rations. Some names drew grain three times. Most weapons were scattered through the chiefs' private storehouses. Yao Chang circled the most outrageous claims and ordered a fresh muster the next day. Yao Shuode warned that strict counting at a time like this would make the tribes think their lord distrusted them.
“They may dislike me,” Yao Chang said, looking beyond the tent. “But don’t make me feed the shadows of thirty thousand men with grain meant for ten thousand.”

They gathered that night to swear an alliance. There were no orderly lines of palace lanterns, only pine torches split beside the river, snapping as they burned. Qiang elders sat in front; former Qin commandants behind them; herdsmen, tenants, and fugitives crowded together. Some raised old Yao blades. Others held nothing but rough wooden clubs. Yao Chang climbed the platform bareheaded, wearing only a leather cloak darkened by smoke.
Someone below cried out that he should proclaim himself king. Yao Chang waited until the voices subsided. “If you call me king today, will you hand your tribes' grain and horses over to me tomorrow?”
The elders made no reply.

“I spent many years in Chang’an. Fu Jian has done good things. Without the Qin registers, how many families of soldiers killed in battle would still have to beg an estate owner for a certificate? Without the mixed army, some men might live all their lives and never serve beneath a banner of their own.”

The crowd stood stunned; some even muttered that he was praising Fu Jian. But he went on. “Your grazing lands cannot be measured with the same rope as tilled fields. Your sons join the army, yet the full household tax is still collected. County clerks insult you and call it the law of Chang’an. You bow before the county gate and those inside pretend to be deaf. Chang’an has beautiful papers enough. Have their edges ever been stained with your blood?”

He called the old herdsman who had lost his land onto the wooden platform. Clutching the old horse-delivery tag, the man recounted in a shaking voice how his son had died. People wept aloud; others drew similar wooden tags from their clothes. His testimony stirred them more deeply than any great proclamation Yao Chang had prepared.

Yao Chang studied their faces in the firelight and at last declared his position. “For all these years the Fu family has held the throne while telling us that the armies of the realm belong to no one surname. If the Heavenly King must always be a Fu, how can the realm believe those words?”

Cheers rolled along the valley. Several chiefs seized the moment to demand the restoration of their old tribal camps and forces, with all merit lands to be divided by the tribes themselves. Yao Chang would not consent at once. He promised that tribes could retain their rites and languages, that those joining him would not be punished merely for their former origins, and that the central camp would audit all grain, weapons, and military achievements. Asked whether their old followers would still recognize them as chiefs, he answered, “Men on campaign will still be led by those who know them. But the central camp must keep a copy of the merit rolls.”
“How is that any different from the Qin army?” someone protested.
Yao Chang hesitated. “I cannot yet give you every answer you want. First we must survive. After the fighting, we can argue about land and banners.”

For a moment the gathering was silent. Some found the admission frank; others realized that this new lord, like the old court, was asking them to trust him before all else. They chose to postpone their doubts until victory. For now the fires blazed, the horses were strong, and the great banner stood before them.

The proclamation was finalized after the assembly. It cited true old cases: pastures seized at Gaoping, arbitrary levies in Anding, favoritism in the army. But among them were rumors that Fu Jian had already died, that Chang’an would deport every Qiang chief, and that the Qin registers would destroy the tribes' ancestral rites. When Yao Shuode read it, he asked whether the latter half ought to be deleted. Yao Chang held his brush motionless for a long time. In the end he changed only “all Qiang people will be slaughtered” to “the tribes stand in mortal peril.”
“My lord knows the palace has announced no death.”
“I know.”
“Then why leave in the claim that the Heavenly King is dead?”
Yao Chang looked at the wet ink on the table. “Chang’an will send fresh reports. People can judge for themselves.”

Even he knew the words did not absolve him. Once news mixed with hatred traveled outward, people heard the thing they feared most first. Any later correction could never catch it. He did not ask the clerk to make a new copy. At dawn the next day, dozens of riders set out with rolled proclamations under their robes, bound for Anding, Beidi, Longxi, and Guanzhong.

Two days later a small Qin garrison town in Anding mutinied. Three unit leaders seized bows and armor and fled west with more than two hundred men. To prevent further defections, the garrison commander Du Yan moved the wives and children of the remaining Qiang soldiers into an old horse yard under guard. The gate soldiers did not want the assignment. Their commander insisted it was only temporary and the families would soon be released. There was no stove in the building, and too little water. On the third night two women came to the gate with their children asking for water and were killed by arrows.

The husband of one woman had joined the rebels. The other woman’s husband was Liang Agui, still serving in the Qin army as the commander of a bow unit. When soldiers came at dawn with the news, he first thought someone was using his family to test his loyalty. Only when he saw his wife’s outer robe did he lean against the wall and slowly sit down. No one dared tell him to bear his grief.

In another county to the east, a magistrate heard the proclamation from White Grass Valley but did not arrest Qiang households. Instead he brought several carts of illegally levied millet back to the county granary, called the taxpayers to check their names in public, and returned what could be returned. Some young men still meant to join Yao Chang. Their fathers asked why they should ride to the valley now that their family’s grain had been restored. After thinking it over, the young men did not mount their horses.

The first western dispatch to reach Chang’an reported only that more than thirty thousand men had gathered at White Grass Valley and several counties had responded. Some members of the imperial clan urged that the families of Qiang soldiers in every garrison be detained at once to prevent more men fleeing west. Fu Hong turned over the report and read the attached casualty list instead. The deaths of the two women had been reduced to four characters: “Mistakenly shot by guards.”
“Who ordered their wives and children locked away?”
“Du Yan.”
“Had those families rebelled?”
“No evidence has been found.”
Fu Hong drew the page from the bundle. “Investigate first. Yao Chang’s rebellion is no reason to put every Qiang family down as members of his camp.”

Fu Rong had sent word from Luoyang about his brother’s illness and remained at the palace there; he could not immediately return to court. After an urgent conference with the chief minister and central army command, the crown prince prepared to ask him to take overall charge of a western expedition. At the same time the pasture disputes were assigned to the censorate and household offices for separate review, with an order that soldiers' families were not to be detained without evidence. The edict was still awaiting verification at the three-seal table when another urgent report arrived from the west: Yao Chang had shifted his forward camp from White Grass Valley toward Anding and sent horsemen ahead to seize the mouth of the valley, closing on Du Yan’s garrison.

Fu Hong lowered his eyes and read Liang Agui’s wife’s name once more. The military situation was urgent, yet the handwriting was remarkably neat. That night he ordered the clerks to place the records of both dead women in the same box as the expedition order, not to file them separately under “minor cases.”
Tomorrow the army would march. The first city gate its banners passed would belong to Qin itself.
